payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Standing on Her Work

¶1 One Tuesday last October, a date-formatting library called tidyclock vanished from the public package registry, and by morning several thousand websites could no longer tell their users what day it was. Its sole maintainer, a retired schoolteacher in Pell Harbor, had deleted it after a decade of unpaid work and one rude bug report too many. Desmond Alcock's new book, Nobody's Job, opens with that night, and it is the right place to begin. I spent nine years maintaining a small text-parsing library used by companies I was never allowed to name, so I read Alcock with the uneasy attention of a patient reading her own chart.

¶2 The book's first half is a diagnosis, and it is a good one. Alcock surveyed four hundred of the most heavily downloaded packages in three programming languages and found that more than half depended on a single active volunteer. He calls these projects load-bearing walls that no inspector has visited, and the metaphor earns its keep: the walls are hidden inside the plaster of every bank, hospital, and school district that runs code on top of them. Nobody chose this arrangement. It accreted, one convenient download at a time, until the whole structure rested on the patience of people who could stop at any moment and owed us nothing if they did.

¶3 It is in the second half, where Alcock turns from diagnosis to cure, that the book loses its footing. His remedy is sponsorship: corporations that profit from open-source software should fund its maintainers, and he describes several foundations that already do so. I will grant that money has saved projects. A stipend kept at least one widely used encryption library alive after its maintainer nearly quit, and Alcock tells that story well. But a stipend changes what the work is. Consider the neighbor who shovels the shared walkway every winter because no one else will; the day you start paying her, the shoveling becomes a service, the snow becomes her problem, and you acquire the right to complain about ice. Sponsorship converts a gift into a contract, and the contract arrives written in the sponsor's priorities, not the project's.

¶4 I know something about how such gifts are received. In nine years I received roughly four thousand bug reports, most of them phrased as demands, several of them threatening, and one, from a hospital network in a city I have never visited, that began with the words "thank you." One. Did any of those four thousand correspondents imagine that a person, rather than a department, was reading them at eleven at night? Alcock understands this loneliness better than any writer I have read, which is precisely why his faith in a check is so puzzling.

¶5 The better cure is already visible in the margins of his own book, though he never names it. The institutions that depend on these libraries do not lack money; they lack a sense that the maintenance is theirs to do. A regional bank runs tidyclock on its login page, employs ninety engineers, and has never assigned one of them a Friday afternoon to review tidyclock's open issues. Volunteer fire departments survive not because the town mails a check to the one person who owns a hose but because the people whose houses would burn show up for the drills. The obligation should attach to dependence, not to profit, and it should be paid in hours, not dollars. This will not rescue every project, and the smallest libraries will still rely on the stubbornness of individuals; but it would spread the weight across the walls that bear it.

¶6 Nobody's Job deserves the wide readership it will probably get. Read it for the first half, which will frighten you in the right way, and argue with the second, which will comfort you in the wrong one. The retired schoolteacher in Pell Harbor did not need a sponsor. She needed the several thousand of us who were standing on her work to notice that we were.

provenance.note: Original review essay of a fictional book, Nobody's Job, by the fictional author Desmond Alcock. All people, institutions, libraries and figures are invented.

blueprint.speaker: Imogen Tarrow, a former volunteer maintainer of a small text-parsing library for nine years, now writing criticism for a general-interest quarterly
blueprint.audience: Educated general readers of a literary and ideas quarterly, most of whom use software built on volunteer-maintained libraries without knowing it, including managers and engineers at the institutions that depend on such code
blueprint.exigence: The publication of Desmond Alcock's book Nobody's Job, which opens with the recent collapse of thousands of websites after the lone maintainer of the tidyclock library deleted it
blueprint.purpose: To recommend the book's diagnosis of fragile volunteer infrastructure while rejecting its prescribed cure of corporate sponsorship, and to propose instead that dependent institutions contribute maintenance labor
blueprint.context: A review essay in The Harrowgate Quarterly, written shortly after a widely noticed outage caused by a single volunteer quitting
blueprint.claim: Alcock is right that critical software rests on unseen, unpaid individuals, but wrong that money is the remedy; the obligation to maintain should attach to dependence and be paid in hours by the institutions that rely on the code.
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Paragraph 1 opens with the tidyclock anecdote and establishes the reviewer's ethos as a former maintainer. Paragraph 2 endorses the book's diagnosis (survey, load-bearing-walls metaphor). Paragraph 3 pivots to the book's prescription, concedes that money has helped, then rebuts with the shoveling analogy: payment converts a gift into a contract. Paragraph 4 shifts to personal testimony about ungrateful bug reports to show that the real deficit is recognition, not cash, and links that back to the critique. Paragraph 5 supplies the alternative cure (institutions lending hours, volunteer fire department analogy) with a qualification of its limits. Paragraph 6 renders the verdict and returns to the schoolteacher of the opening.

devices.function: Opens with the concrete tidyclock collapse to dramatize the stakes and introduce the book's starting point
Establishes the reviewer's standing as a former maintainer who reads the book from inside the problem
Reports Alcock's survey finding to support the diagnosis that most heavily used packages depend on one volunteer
Load-bearing walls figure the hidden, unexamined dependence of institutions on volunteer code; returned to in the proposal to spread the weight
Colons set up the explanation of the metaphor and the statement of Alcock's remedy
Very short sentences after long ones isolate key points: no one chose the arrangement; only one thank-you
Shift from appreciative to critical at paragraph 3, then from analytical to personal and wry at paragraph 4
Grants that stipends have saved projects before rebutting that payment changes the nature of the work
Shoveling the shared walkway shows how payment converts a gift into a service; volunteer fire departments model obligation attached to dependence
Gift versus contract, hours versus dollars, frighten versus comfort sharpen the reviewer's distinctions
Presses readers to recognize that they may have treated a person as a department
The one-word sentence One. wryly registers the scarcity of gratitude without complaint
Limits the proposal's scope so it cannot be dismissed as a cure-all
Instructs the reader how to read the book, delivering the verdict
Parallel clauses build the consequences of payment and balance the two halves of the verdict

blueprint.counterargument: Alcock's position, and the reviewer's own concession, that corporate sponsorship money has in fact rescued projects such as an encryption library; the reviewer grants this and rebuts that payment turns a gift into a contract shaped by the sponsor's priorities.

options.text: suggesting that maintainers are too easily wounded to be trusted with critical infrastructure

The account of demanding reports is followed by a question asking whether any correspondent imagined 'a person, rather than a department' was reading them, and the essay closes by naming 'the several thousand of us who were standing on her work'; the audience of ordinary users is being implicated in the neglect.
"suggesting that maintainers are too easily wounded to be trusted with critical infrastructure" is incorrect: The passage's sympathy runs toward maintainers and against those who make demands of them; it faults the dependents, not the volunteers.
"demonstrating that hospital networks are more considerate users of volunteer code than banks or corporations" is incorrect: The single hospital thank-you is used as a rarity, not as a comparison among institutional types; the passage never ranks hospitals against banks.
"establishing the technical authority she needs to challenge the findings of Alcock's survey" is incorrect: She does not challenge the survey; she endorses the diagnosis in paragraph 2. The anecdote concerns recognition and loneliness, not technical credentials.

"emphasizing that only one institution was actually using the writer's library" is incorrect: The 'one' counts thank-you messages, not users; the previous sentence establishes thousands of correspondents, and paragraph 1 refers to companies she could not name.

issues.issue: The passage never says why contributed hours avoid the gift-into-contract problem the reviewer attributes to money. The volunteer fire department analogy only implies it.
The move from the bug-report testimony (recognition is the deficit) to the proposal of institutional hours is somewhat implicit. A sentence tying the two would tighten the line of reasoning.
The volunteer fire department analogy is slightly idealized, since many such departments also receive public funding. It works as an analogy about participation by those who depend on the service.
The stray 'ALTON original passage' label precedes the title and should be removed before publication.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Proposal to Keep Brindle Creek Park Free

[1] Parks are something that most people have an opinion about. [2] Last month the Halvering Parks Commission announced that it is considering a 3-dollar entry fee at Brindle Creek Park to cover a 41,000-dollar maintenance shortfall. [3] As treasurer of the Halvering High student council, I am writing on behalf of our 38 members to ask the commission to vote against the fee at its May meeting. [4] Free parks are good for Halvering in a lot of ways.

[5] First, the fee would raise less money than it appears to. [6] Our council surveyed 212 students and parents outside the park gate on two Saturdays in April. [7] Sixty-four percent said they would visit less often if the fee were adopted, and 29 percent said they would stop coming altogether. [8] Fewer visitors would also mean fewer customers on Kettle Street, where the owner of Marron's Bakery told us that weekend park traffic brings in roughly a third of her sales. [9] The commission's projection counts on 60,000 paid entries a year, but that figure assumes attendance stays flat.

[10] Second, a free park can be cheaper to maintain than the commission's numbers suggest. [11] Our council already organizes a fall cleanup that drew 90 volunteers last October. [12] We propose expanding it into a monthly Saturday crew, supervised by parks staff, that handles litter pickup, mulching, and repainting the picnic shelters. [13] The commission's own report prices those three tasks at 17,000 dollars a year in contractor costs. [14] Students love being outside, so they will definitely show up. [15] Turning down that much free labor would be a pretty dumb move.

[16] Brindle Creek Park is where the cross-country team trains, where the kindergarten classes count ducks, and where my grandfather plays chess on Thursdays. [17] We ask the commission to keep the gate open and to let us help pay for it with our Saturdays. [18] Thank you for considering this proposal.

el_passage.title: Proposal to Keep Brindle Creek Park Free
paragraphs: Parks are something that most people have an opinion about.
Last month the Halvering Parks Commission announced that it is considering a 3-dollar entry fee at Brindle Creek Park to cover a 41,000-dollar maintenance shortfall.
As treasurer of the Halvering High student council, I am writing on behalf of our 38 members to ask the commission to vote against the fee at its May meeting.
Free parks are good for Halvering in a lot of ways.
First, the fee would raise less money than it appears to.
Our council surveyed 212 students and parents outside the park gate on two Saturdays in April.
Sixty-four percent said they would visit less often if the fee were adopted, and 29 percent said they would stop coming altogether.
Fewer visitors would also mean fewer customers on Kettle Street, where the owner of Marron's Bakery told us that weekend park traffic brings in roughly a third of her sales.
The commission's projection counts on 60,000 paid entries a year, but that figure assumes attendance stays flat.
Second, a free park can be cheaper to maintain than the commission's numbers suggest.
Our council already organizes a fall cleanup that drew 90 volunteers last October.
We propose expanding it into a monthly Saturday crew, supervised by parks staff, that handles litter pickup, mulching, and repainting the picnic shelters.
The commission's own report prices those three tasks at 17,000 dollars a year in contractor costs.
Students love being outside, so they will definitely show up.
Turning down that much free labor would be a pretty dumb move.
Brindle Creek Park is where the cross-country team trains, where the kindergarten classes count ducks, and where my grandfather plays chess on Thursdays.
We ask the commission to keep the gate open and to let us help pay for it with our Saturdays.
Thank you for considering this proposal.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 1 with an opening sentence that presents a concrete scene showing what is at stake in the commission's vote and that is consistent with the details given later in the draft. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Across the country, towns of every size have debated whether public parks should charge visitors for entry.
options.why: It is a generalization about towns everywhere rather than a concrete scene at Brindle Creek Park, so it does not show what is at stake locally.
options.label: too_broad

options.label: correct

options.text: The commission should reject the entry fee because the fee would raise less than expected and volunteers could reduce costs.
options.why: It states the argument's thesis rather than presenting a scene, so it does not accomplish the writer's stated goal for the opening.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
The Gearhounds: A First-Season Report

[1] Last August, eleven students and one chemistry teacher met in the back corner of the woodshop at Harlow Creek High School with a donated toolbox, two secondhand motor kits, and no idea how to build a robot. [2] Eight months later, our robot, which we named Marmalade because of its orange zip ties, placed ninth out of twenty-six teams at the Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore. [3] This report is about what the Gearhounds did this year and some things that happened. [4] I am writing it because the Student Activities Board asked every new club for a summary before it votes on next year's budgets.

[5] The team spent September and October learning basics: how to wire a motor controller, how to read a gear ratio, how to keep a chassis from twisting. [6] Our first drive base, finished in November, could not turn left. [7] Instead of starting over, we traced the problem to a mismatched pair of wheels and swapped them in a single afternoon. [8] By February, Marmalade could lift a foam block, drive over a ramp, and park itself inside a taped square, the three tasks the competition required. [9] Honestly, the judges were kind of blown away that a first-year team even showed up with a working bot.

[10] The members learned a great deal from the season. [11] Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day. [12] Our faculty adviser, Ms. Delacroix-Tam, kept a sign-in sheet, and attendance never dropped below nine members, even during exam week.

[13] Next year the team needs a locking storage cabinet, a second set of batteries, and roughly 900 dollars for competition registration. [14] The board should fund us because robotics is obviously the coolest club at the school and everyone knows it. [15] We are not asking for a new room or a new teacher; we are asking for a shelf, a charger, and a chance to finish what we started.

paragraphs: Last August, eleven students and one chemistry teacher met in the back corner of the woodshop at Harlow Creek High School with a donated toolbox, two secondhand motor kits, and no idea how to build a robot.
Eight months later, our robot, which we named Marmalade because of its orange zip ties, placed ninth out of twenty-six teams at the Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore.
This report is about what the Gearhounds did this year and some things that happened.
I am writing it because the Student Activities Board asked every new club for a summary before it votes on next year's budgets.
The team spent September and October learning basics: how to wire a motor controller, how to read a gear ratio, how to keep a chassis from twisting.
Our first drive base, finished in November, could not turn left.
Instead of starting over, we traced the problem to a mismatched pair of wheels and swapped them in a single afternoon.
By February, Marmalade could lift a foam block, drive over a ramp, and park itself inside a taped square, the three tasks the competition required.
Honestly, the judges were kind of blown away that a first-year team even showed up with a working bot.
The members learned a great deal from the season.
Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day.
Our faculty adviser, Ms. Delacroix-Tam, kept a sign-in sheet, and attendance never dropped below nine members, even during exam week.
Next year the team needs a locking storage cabinet, a second set of batteries, and roughly 900 dollars for competition registration.
The board should fund us because robotics is obviously the coolest club at the school and everyone knows it.
We are not asking for a new room or a new teacher; we are asking for a shelf, a charger, and a chance to finish what we started.

blueprint.purpose: A year-end report from a student team captain to the school's Student Activities Board, which will vote on whether to fund the robotics club for a second year
blueprint.audience: The Harlow Creek High School Student Activities Board: a faculty-and-student committee that allocates club budgets and values participation, learning outcomes, and careful use of money
blueprint.claim: In its first season the Gearhounds built a working robot, turned beginners into capable builders, and need only modest funding to continue
blueprint.genre: report on a school project draft
blueprint.theme: the first season of a school robotics team
blueprint.speaker: Teodor Vasquez-Lindqvist, a tenth grader and captain of the Gearhounds robotics team
blueprint.exigence: The Student Activities Board asked every new club for a summary before its budget vote
blueprint.context: The team began in August in the woodshop with donated equipment and competed in April at the fictional Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Narrative opening establishes starting point and result; paragraph 2 traces the build process and a solved problem; paragraph 3 asserts learning and attendance; paragraph 4 lists needs and closes with a plea
blueprint.counterargument: Not addressed in the draft; the board might see a new club as an unproven expense

devices.function: Frames the season as a before-and-after story to make the result vivid
Shows the sequence of the build so the board can see steady progress
Links a failure to a diagnosed cause to show problem-solving
Contrasts a large request with a small one to make the ask seem modest
